1:
Henry reads the date as the proof of the hour: the fourth monarchy stood at its height, Judea had become a province and was taxed with the rest, and the temple of Janus was shut, so the sceptre had departed from Judah and Shiloh must come. Bede makes the peace itself the sign, there being no greater token of it than the whole world brought under one taxing, and hears a literal fulfilment of the swords beaten into ploughshares. Calvin sets human contrivance aside: Joseph and Mary had no design but to obey the edict, and were led like blind persons by the hand of God to the place where Christ must be born. He presses the irony twice: an ungodly man seizes what God was accustomed to demand of his people, and the officer executing Caesar's commission is, unknown to himself, God's herald calling Mary to Bethlehem.

The fathers read the enrolment as a figure. Ambrose finds a secular registration implying a spiritual, a census of souls laid before the King not of earth but of heaven, the old census of the Synagogue abolished and a new one of the Church preparing; and asks who could demand the registering of the whole world but the one whose the earth is, noting that the just man and the virgin came up to it, he who kept the word and she who obeyed it. Origen sees a kind of sacrament in it: Christ's name being written with all, he might sanctify all. Gregory calls the registering mystical, since he appeared in the flesh who should write down the names of his own elect in eternity. Theophylact adds that one king rules the world because at Christ's coming the worship of many gods should cease. Leo turns it to the hearer: there is one common measure of joy, so the saint may exult, the sinner be glad, the gentile take courage.

On the reach of the decree the moderns divide. Barnes would render it the whole land, meaning Palestine, since no such taxing of all the world is mentioned by any ancient writer and Luke's account demands no more, world being elsewhere used in just this limited sense. Clarke agrees the Romans had no right to levy where their dominion did not reach, shows from Polybius and Plutarch that the word was used of the Roman government, and restrains it to Judea, as the Septuagint does. Ellicott keeps the Roman empire, as throughout the New Testament, and answers the silence of the historians from the policy of Augustus, who took such returns about every ten years and laid a survey of the empire before the Senate. Robertson insists it was a census and not a taxing, and reports that papyri and inscriptions have confirmed Luke on every point here.

The governor's name is the harder knot: Quirinus is not named as governor of Syria until some twelve years later. Barnes follows Lardner in making it the first census of the man afterwards familiarly known as governor, and defends the idiom by noting that one may say General Washington saved Braddock's army. Clarke offers that, and a second reading, that the word rendered first may mean before, as where John says he was before me; he prefers the second. Ellicott refuses it, the construction being absent from Luke elsewhere and unnatural across twelve years; he supplies a missing governor from a coin of Antioch, shows Quirinus already in office in the East, and emphasises the adjective: this enrolment was the first under his government. Robertson appeals to Ramsay for a fourteen-year census cycle in Egypt and inscriptions proving Quirinus twice in Syria. Calvin suspects Josephus's recollection simply failed him, and adds that the edict may have been delayed by tumult, Coponius being sent with an army. Lightfoot sets out Dion Cassius and then leaves it: let the more learned judge.
6:
Gregory of Nyssa holds the birth not wholly subject to the laws of our nature, the burden light and the delivery without pain, since she who engrafted death was condemned to bring forth in trouble, and she who brought life should be delivered with joy. On the word firstborn the witnesses part. Jerome answers Helvidius by distinguishing: every only-begotten is firstborn, but not every firstborn only-begotten, the firstborn being not he whom others follow but he before whom there is none. Bede divides the title instead, only-begotten in the substance of divinity, firstborn in the taking of humanity, firstborn in grace and only-begotten in nature. Barnes says plainly that the obvious meaning is that she had other children, and Robertson that there is not a particle of evidence for the contrary notion.

The swaddling and the manger are read as a series of exchanges. Bede sets them out: he who clothes the whole world with its varied beauty is wrapped in common linen that we might receive the best robe; he is folded hand and foot that our hands might be raised to good work; and he who sits at the Father's right hand finds no room in an inn, that he might prepare many mansions. The Greek Exposition wonders at the straitening undergone by one who holds the world in his hands, and finds him seeking poverty from the beginning and ennobling it in himself. Chrysostom adds that he might have come moving the heavens and shooting thunderbolts, but his desire was to save and to trample on human pride from its birth. Cyril makes the manger the place of food, that men grown like the beasts might partake not of hay but of heavenly bread.

The furniture of the scene is reconstructed carefully. Barnes explains that the word rendered inn means only a halting place, a khan or caravanserai, and puts Joseph and Mary in one of the recesses off the stable, down to the unfurnished cells and the cloth stretched across for privacy. Clarke shows from Wetstein that the word means not the crib but the whole stable, and quotes Virgil on horses standing in lofty stables. Ellicott reports the tradition of a cave, which Justin Martyr read as fulfilling a prophecy of a place of defence in a lofty rock, notes that limestone caves were commonly used as stables, traces the ox and the ass of the paintings to a fanciful reading of Isaiah, and identifies the inn as the lodging of Chimham, built by the son of Barzillai. Lightfoot and Gill both report the Arabian who told a Jew the Redeemer was born, naming Menahem son of Hezekiah at Birath Arba; and Lightfoot, unable to say what the place was, decides a man had better hold his tongue than conjecture to no purpose.

Whether any of this proves the family poor is disputed. Calvin sees both the great poverty of Joseph and a tyranny which compelled him to bring his wife at so inconvenient a season, and supposes the royal line was handled the more harshly; Joseph, unable to avoid it, bows his head and commends himself to God. Henry counts the stable an instance of his parents' poverty and of the manners of the age, since men with any common humanity would not have turned a woman in travail into a stable. Clarke objects outright: the reason given is that there was no room, and an honest man blessed in his business could not have been unable to procure a night's lodging, nor would he have brought his wife at all had he been so ill fitted for the journey. Barnes takes the middle way, that being there proved nothing but necessity, while Jesus was nevertheless born poor and cradled in no palace. Wesley only remarks that now also there is seldom room for Christ in an inn.
8:
Chrysostom observes that the angel came to Joseph in a dream, as to one easily brought to believe, and to the shepherds in visible shape, as to men of a ruder nature; he sought no scribes, who were tormented with envy, there being a road which leads by innocence to philosophy. Bede notes that nowhere in the Old Testament do angels appear by day, the privilege being kept for the hour when a light arose in the darkness, and sets the sides together: he is sent forth from the womb but shines from heaven, lies in a common inn but lives in celestial light. Henry adds that the chief priests were not prepared for the tidings, and that the shepherds were neither asleep nor at their devotions but at their calling. Calvin grants the method looks unsuitable, and makes that the point: the treasure is deposited in earthen vessels, so let us not be ashamed of instructors taken from among the dung of cattle.

The flocks in the open supply the chapter's one chronological datum. Lightfoot identifies them as the sheep of the wilderness, driven out about the Passover and brought home at the first rain in Marchesvan. Clarke concludes that the nativity in December should on this ground be given up, and reports from Fabricius a hundred and thirty-six opinions about the year, the day having been placed in every month, until Pope Julius fixed on the twenty-fifth, which the Romans kept as the feast of Bruma. Ellicott takes the season just before the Passover, when the grass is greenest, notes that the traditional date appears only in the fourth century and may have been chosen to displace the Saturnalia, and adds from the Mishna that the temple's sacrificial sheep were pastured in these fields, so that men lately rejoicing over the Paschal lambs heard now of the Lamb of God. Barnes agrees it was probably earlier, then stops: what God regards as unimportant he conceals.

On the message the witnesses divide the three titles. The Greek Exposition refers Saviour to the action and Lord to the dignity of the person, and observes that the angel not only soothes terror but pours in gladness. Cyril takes the middle name as the ground of adoration, signifying not the nature but the compound substance of two natures, and distinguishes the anointing from the figurative kind poured on kings, or on Cyrus the idolater. Bede marks what the sign was: not Tyrian purple and a gilded couch, but poor swaddling clothes and a manger. Gregory finds the watching rewarded, since those see sublime things who watch over their flocks. Calvin presses the pronoun, since it would give no delight to hear the Author of salvation is born unless each believed he was born for him.

The hymn draws out its grammar and its sense. Bede explains the multitude by saying a single angel's authority might have seemed small, and hears the host wishing peace to men once despised as abject and now esteemed as friends. Chrysostom sets the change against the old errands, when angels were sent to punish Israel and David and Sodom, where now they sing thanksgiving, God having brought angels down to men and men up to heaven. Origen raises the objection that the Lord says he came not to send peace on earth, and answers that the peace withheld is not the peace of good will. Lightfoot takes good will toward men for the subject and the rest for the predicate: that good will is glory to God in the highest and peace on earth. Ellicott and Robertson both prefer the genitive of the oldest manuscripts, peace among men of good will, who are the objects of God's approval; Ellicott refuses the softer rendering, peace to men of peace, and adds that the clause has no verb and may be read as proclamation or prayer.
15:
Bede fastens on what the shepherds said, that they would see not the child but the word which had come to pass, so the errand is to see how the Word was made flesh. Ambrose remarks how exactly Scripture weighs each term, since in beholding the flesh of the Lord we behold the Word, warns that their humble character makes this no slight example of faith, simplicity being sought and not pride, and adds that no one indolently seeks after Christ. The Greek Exposition has them leave the sheepfolds and set out by night after the Saviour's light. Calvin notes that they were never expressly commanded to go and went because they knew God's design: the word must not pass away with the sound, and they exhort one another, since it is not enough that each attend to his own duty.

What they found was in itself an offence. Calvin calls the sight revolting and enough of itself to produce aversion, nothing being less probable than that the King of the whole people should be one unworthy to rank with the lowest; yet the glory of God was so before their eyes that their faith rose above everything mean in Christ. Origen reads the three they found as the mother who brought Jesus into the world, the guardian of the birth, and the Saviour himself, and calls it the manger Israel knew not, where the ox knows his owner. Ellicott grants the adoration is implied though not stated, and assigns the ox and the ass of the pictures, with the light glowing from the cradle, to the apocryphal legends.

All the commentators make the shepherds the first preachers. Clarke asks what their text was and answers from the hymn, glory to God and peace and good will among men, then turns it against the crusades and against wars for religion as an insult to the gospel. Barnes says they now had evidence that would satisfy others, and makes it a duty of the newly converted to tell what they have seen and felt. Bede says the shepherds of the Church were ordained to this end, that what they learn in the Scriptures they explain to their hearers, and extends the office to every private man who rules his good actions with due moderation. The Gloss marvels at the attestation itself, by men who could not have devised such things but were proclaiming truth with simple eloquence. Calvin agrees their low rank diminished their credit, and observes that though all were astonished not one moved a step, so the report left the people's ignorance inexcusable.

On Mary's silence the readings converge. Ambrose has her faith increased by the shepherds, and bids us learn the chastity of the Virgin, no less chaste in her words than in her body, gathering into her heart the materials of faith. Bede keeps her to the laws of virgin modesty, divulging the secrets of Christ to none but comparing what she had read in prophecy with what she now saw. The Greek Exposition collects her whole store, whatever the angel had said and whatever she heard from Zacharias and Elisabeth and the shepherds, and finds that on comparison she perceived one harmony. Clarke takes the word for weighing in its Latin sense, each new circumstance measured against those past, and Barnes calls it a delicate expression of a mother's feelings. Robertson keeps the imperfect, a keeping together that did not stop, and wonders whether Mary kept a baby book that Luke may have seen. Henry adds that the truths of Christ are worth keeping and the way to keep them safe is to ponder them, meditation being the best help to memory. Calvin ends on the return: if the cradle raised these men from the stable to heaven, how much more should the death and resurrection raise us.
21:
Epiphanius gives four reasons: to show the reality of the flesh against those who said he came in appearance only, to prove the body not of one substance with the Deity nor descended from heaven as Valentinian said, to confirm a rite he had himself instituted, and to leave the Jews no excuse for refusing an uncircumcised Christ. Against Ebion and Cerinthus, who argued that disciples must therefore be circumcised, he turns their premise: if Christ is mere man, a boy can no more cause his own circumcision than any infant. Origen answers them otherwise, that as we died and rose with him so with him were we circumcised, and need none in the flesh. Bede makes it an example of obedience and a compassion on men unable to bear the law, circumcision having brought to original sin the cure baptism brings now, save that the circumcised waited in a blessed rest outside the kingdom.

Cyril ties the day to the rising, since on the eighth day Christ rose and conveyed a spiritual circumcision, the name being imposed on the same day. Bede finds the precedent in Abraham, who on the day of his circumcision was thought worthy of an increase of his name, and carries it to the elect, that as from Christ they are called Christians so from the Saviour they may be called saved. Henry presses the legal force: by it he made himself a debtor to the whole law, circumcision being, as Doctor Goodwin says, the bond by which we acknowledged ourselves debtors, to which Christ set his hand; and a circumcision at eight days, he argues, makes far more for dedicating the infant seed of the church than a baptism at thirty makes for deferring it.

Whether Mary needed purifying is pressed from both sides. Bede finds her exempt, since not every woman who brings forth but she who has received seed is pronounced unclean, so that she submitted of her own will; Titus agrees that having conceived of the Holy Spirit she was free from all uncleanness. Calvin refuses to read the law as merely political, holding it set before the Jews the corruption of their nature and proves original sin of itself, since the Lord declares the child comes from its mother polluted; and the fountain of purity chose to be reckoned unclean to wash away our stains. Ellicott grants neither rite was here necessary and explains the act as simple obedience, the mystery of the birth not yet being revealed to her. Clarke makes it practical: had she not kept the days she could not have appeared in public worship and would have passed for an apostate, and uncircumcised he would have had no Jewish hearers.

The two birds are read at length. Bede offers several keys: the pigeon denotes simplicity and the turtle dove chastity, since having lost her mate she heeds not to find another; or the turtle is solitary and the pigeon flies in flocks, one pointing to the secret tears of confession and the other to the public assembling of the Church, or one to the contemplative and the other to the active life. Luke, he observes, purposely omits which was offered, so as not to prefer one life before the other. Gregory of Nyssa finds the law of the opened womb peculiarly fulfilled, since he alone opened a womb till then unopened and left its seal after the birth. Lightfoot reports that this was the offering of the poor, which a rich man offering did not do his duty, and that King Agrippa, coming with a thousand burnt offerings, was prevented by a poor man with two turtledoves. Clarke and Ellicott take the substitution as proof the family was not in affluence, while Calvin meets the objection from the Magi's gold by answering that we do not read of camels laden with it.
25:
Who Simeon was is canvassed and left open. Clarke reports that several learned men make him Hillel's son and president of the grand Sanhedrin. Ellicott develops it, naming him the father of Gamaliel, and finds it suggestive that the Mishna passes his name over, as though he stood under a cloud for believing in the prophet of Nazareth; but he sets against it that Luke's manner implies a man of very advanced age awaiting his departure, and concludes that the name was so common that all conjectures are precarious. Lightfoot clears away the Simeon the Just of the Jewish histories, grants that Rabban Simeon the son of Hillel was living at Jerusalem in those years, and remarks that nothing is recited from him in the Mishna, which he calls very extraordinary and cannot explain. Barnes allows only that nothing is certainly known of him.

His character and his hope are read together. Ambrose observes that righteousness is scarcely preserved without fear, not the fear that dreads the loss of worldly goods, which perfect love casts out, but the holy fear by which a man grows the more careful not to offend as his love grows ardent. Gregory of Nyssa denies that what he awaited was worldly happiness, taking it for a passing over to the beauty of truth from the shadow of the law. Calvin makes it a doctrine of the remnant, since nearly the whole nation was profane and within this small band lay the Church of God, while the priests and scribes claimed the title; all had the Messiah's name on their lips, but hardly one endured present affliction in the assurance that redemption was at hand.

The taking of the child into the arms is where the fathers press hardest. Origen bids a man who would hold Jesus have the Spirit for guide and come to the temple, and puts Simeon's release in those hands: as long as he held not Christ he was in prison. Theophylact hears in the address an acknowledgement that the child in those arms is Lord of life and death, and so God. Basil adds that if you examine the words of the righteous you find them all sorrowing over this world and its mournful delay. Bede makes the exchange visible, the righteous man under the law receiving the infant to signify that the righteousness of works was to give place to the lowly but saving grace of faith, and the old man receiving the child to show that a world worn with age should return to childlike innocence. Cyril keeps the paradox plain: the Legislator is subject to his own decrees, and paid the half shekel though as Son he owed no tax, so a man who sees him keeping the law should not be offended but reflect on the plan of salvation.

The song itself is taken clause by clause. The Greek Exposition notes the promise fulfilled, since he was to see the Lord's Christ before he saw death, and now neither dismay at its taste nor doubting thoughts remain. Ellicott and Robertson both press the words for Lord and for departing, which belong to the manumission of a slave, so Simeon speaks as one set free, after weary years on the watch-tower of expectation, by the rising sun. Gregory of Nyssa calls blessed the eyes of his soul and body alike, and marks the widening: a man waiting for the consolation of Israel cries out on obtaining it that he has seen the salvation of all people. Bede notes that the enlightening of the Gentiles is rightly set before the glory of Israel, because when their fullness has come in then shall Israel be safe. Calvin warns against those who plead this example and boast they would die willingly if this or that were granted first, since Simeon had a promise and they have only their wishes.
33:
Bede explains the title of father, held not because Joseph was the real one, as the Photinians say, but because out of regard for Mary all men took him so. The Greek Exposition notes that Simeon blessed them both but gave the presage only to the mother, so as neither to strip Joseph of the likeness of a father nor leave her unnamed as the true one. Calvin raises the difficulty that the less is blessed of the greater, and answers that the apostle means only the priestly blessing, Simeon having prayed as a private man for the advancement of Christ's kingdom, as the Psalms prescribe.

The fall and the rising are read at several depths. Origen gives the plain sense, a fall of unbelievers and a rising of believers, then unsettles it: no one falls who was not before standing, so who stood, for whose fall he came? He answers from his own case, that while he stood in sin it was good for him to fall and die to sin. Gregory of Nyssa distinguishes salvation, prepared before the face of all people, from the falling and raising, which is of many, and applies the fall chiefly to Israel, who must forfeit ancient privileges for refusing one who had come forth from them. Chrysostom makes the rising a change of life, since when the sensual man becomes chaste and the covetous merciful a resurrection takes place, and notes that the sun is the more trying to weak sight the brighter it shines. Barnes insists the word again is not in the Greek, so the same persons are not meant to fall and rise, while Ellicott allows that some may fall first and then, though sorely bruised, rise. Robertson sums it: Judas despairs, Peter repents; one robber blasphemes, the other confesses.

On the sign the witnesses agree that it means the cross. Basil says so outright, Moses having made a brazen serpent and set it for a sign, and a sign betokening something marvellous. Gregory of Nyssa finds honour and dishonour joined, the same token being venerated by some and received by others as absurd and monstrous. Origen puts the contradiction not in believers, who know that all written of him is true, but in unbelievers, with whom everything written of him is a sign spoken against. Clarke takes it for a mark or butt to shoot at, a metaphor from archers, or else the ensign to which the Gentiles were to seek while the Jews rejected it. Calvin uses the same archer's mark for a general verdict, that the harmony of the world in opposing the gospel shows a natural enmity, men not conspiring so exactly without it.

The sword is the chapter's hardest crux, and four readings stand. Lightfoot takes it for a prediction of martyrdom, thy soul meaning thy life, and cites Epiphanius, who allows that whether she died or was put to death she has a crown among the martyrs. Gill offers the spear of scandal, the calumny she would meet for conceiving unmarried, then the sorrows that reached her from cradle to cross. Clarke leans to martyrdom but grants that respectable Greek writers use the figure for pungent sorrow. Bede refuses that reading, since no history tells of her being slain, and since iron kills the body and not the soul it must be the grief of the passion, which she could not watch unmoved even while certain he would overcome death. Ambrose takes the sword for the word of God, sharper than the sharpest, and so a proof of her wisdom. Ellicott and Robertson identify the weapon as the long Thracian javelin, not the short Roman blade, and Robertson calls the clause a thorn among their roses. Calvin ends on the revealing of thoughts, the lurking-places of human dissimulation being so deep that they stay hidden until Christ comes with his light.
36:
Ambrose fits Anna into a series: Simeon had prophesied, a wife had prophesied, a virgin had prophesied, and it was meet a widow should prophesy, that no condition should be wanting. Origen judges that long chastity and fasting made her worthy of prophecy, and accounts for the silence about her words by making Simeon the character of the law, whose name means obedience, and Anna the character of grace, which her name means, so that Christ came between them and Simeon departed with the law while Anna was sustained living on. Bede reads her mystically as the Church, widowed by her Husband's death, the eighty-four years being seven times twelve, seven for the course of this world and twelve for apostolic teaching.

Whether she was strictly a prophetess, and how old, are both disputed. Clarke denies the strict sense, taking her for a holy woman whose knowledge fitted her to instruct others, since prophesying is speaking to edification, and makes the eighty-four her whole age. Robertson gives the word its old sense of a woman who interprets oracles and, reckoning the eighty-four as widowhood, reports her at a hundred and six. Calvin leaves the reckoning doubtful and presses another point, that two persons in whom the Spirit dwelt deserve more reverence than a multitude swelled with empty titles. Ellicott finds it remarkable that a woman should be a prophetess when no man was recognised as a prophet, and draws from her tribe that Aser, though carried into exile among the ten, was not altogether lost, its members keeping their genealogies. Lightfoot adds that she was a Galilean, which bears awkwardly on the saying that out of Galilee arises no prophet.

The return to Nazareth forces the harmony with Matthew, and the witnesses take five ways. Bede says Luke omitted what he knew Matthew had set forth, the flight into Egypt and the return after Herod's death, and observes that each Evangelist leaves out what he knows another will relate, so a careful reader finds the gaps only by comparison. The Greek Exposition puts this verse before the descent into Egypt, the going up to Bethlehem having been only for the taxing, so that when it was done they went down to Nazareth of their own accord. Barnes agrees they returned but not immediately, defending the compression by the parallel of Paul, said to have come to Jerusalem on his conversion when three years had passed. Clarke supposes a return to Galilee at once and a second return after Egypt. Ellicott doubts that either Evangelist knew the other's narrative, each writing from what he heard, and says plainly that they cannot readily be harmonised, where Robertson holds that the two Gospels supplement each other. Calvin refuses outright the notion that the family settled at Bethlehem, calling it foolish to credit Joseph with an abode in a town where he could not find a lodging for a night.

On the growth the fathers guard both natures. Theophylact observes that he might have come from the womb at full stature, but that this would have looked imaginary, and that wisdom displayed in infancy would have seemed a prodigy, whereas a gradual showing filled the world; he insists the strengthening in spirit is no receiving of wisdom, since what is most perfect at the beginning cannot become more perfect. Cyril joins the increase in wisdom to the increase in age, the divine nature unfolding its wisdom in proportion to bodily growth. Bede distinguishes the terms, wisdom because in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, grace because it was given the man Christ Jesus to be from the first both perfect man and perfect God, the Word himself needing no strengthening. Henry contrasts other children, who have foolishness bound in their hearts and show the corruption of their nature, where nothing but the grace of God was upon him.
41:
Gill notes that Joseph was bound to the three feasts while the women were not, the passover of women being voluntary. Henry makes the yearly journey a lesson, since they were poor and the way long, and had a son in the house able to teach them better than all the rabbins at Jerusalem, yet went up. Ellicott sets out the stages of Jewish childhood, the weaning at three, the Law at five, a direct responsibility at twelve and the phylacteries at thirteen, calling it an epoch of transition like our own confirmation; and if the birth fell at the Paschal season the boy may have completed his thirteenth year during this feast.

Whether he stayed behind by design is disputed. The Greek Exposition says he tarried secretly so that his parents should not hinder the discussion with the lawyers, and so that he might neither be kept away nor be disobedient. Ellicott denies the design: the words do not imply it, and the probable course was that he went as usual when the feast was over while Joseph and Mary took for granted he had started with the other boys from Nazareth, so that he was left in the city, finding shelter where they had lodged. Robertson agrees it was no disobedience but an intense interest in the temple services, an involuntary preoccupation that held him fast. Epiphanius draws a doctrinal point from the age: at twelve and not at thirty Christ is already the astonishment of all men, so none may say the Spirit came at the baptism and made him the Christ, since from his childhood he acknowledged both the temple and his Father.

How a day could pass before he was missed is explained, then pressed. Bede supplies the custom, that men and women travelled separately while the children went with either parent indifferently, so each thought in turn that the child was with the other. Clarke gives the same account, then turns on them: knowing what a treasure they possessed, how could they be so long without looking on it, and where were the bowels and tender solicitude of the mother? Let them answer who can. Barnes offers three considerations instead, that families and neighbours joined into a large company, that Jesus was probably with them while they prepared to start, and that part of the company may have gone ahead and been overtaken only at night. Robertson describes the caravan and quotes Plummer, that the Nazareth company was so long it took a day to look through. Calvin sees no reason to wonder at the first day, and holds that their later conduct shows it was not indolence or carelessness.

The three days are counted and then read. The Gloss offers a figure, that the advent looked for by the patriarchs before the Law was not found, nor that sought by the prophets under the Law, but only that which the Gentiles seek under grace. Origen presses where he was not: not among kinsfolk, since human relations could not comprehend the Son of God, nor among acquaintance, since he passes beyond all human knowledge; so seek him in the temple, among the masters who are in it, and seek with labour and sorrow, for many seek carelessly who never find him. Ambrose makes the three days a sign that after three days of victorious suffering he who was believed dead should rise. Lightfoot reports that the first day's journey from Jerusalem was thirty miles to Neapolis, while the spot shown to travellers as the place where the child was missed lies ten miles out, and leaves it there: you may believe those that show it as you think fit. Henry turns the search into counsel, that whoever has lost his comforts in Christ should bethink himself where and when he lost them and return where he last had them.
46:
Lightfoot asks where in the temple this happened, listing three courts of judicature and a synagogue, and remarks that those who undertake to show the spot where the parents missed him may tell us which; he adds that it is hard to say what place a boy could be admitted to among the doctors. Origen divides the posture: because he was the Son of God he is in the midst of the doctors enlightening them, but because he was a little child he is found asking and not teaching, to set an example that wise children should hear their masters rather than teach them; yet he asked not to learn but that in asking he might instruct. Chrysostom observes that the Lord did no miracle in his childhood, and that Luke records this one fact which made men wonder.

The Greek Exposition has her make a mournful inquiry in everything like a mother, with confidence and humility and affection, and has the Lord set all at rest by correcting her word about his reputed father and manifesting his true one. Origen notes that she knew he was not Joseph's son and yet calls her husband his father, and asks why they sought him sorrowing, since they could not dread the loss of one they knew to be the Lord; they sought, he answers, as a man searches the Scriptures with pains, not supposing them to have erred but anxious to find the truth. Bede holds that he blames them not for seeking him as their son but compels them to raise their minds higher. Robertson adds Alford's note, that up to this time Joseph had been so called by the holy child himself and from this time never.

What he claimed to be doing is the chapter's last crux. Robertson is flat: the words mean in my Father's house, not about my Father's business, and the pronoun is my and not our; they are the first words of Jesus preserved to us, a crisp idiom expressing amazement that his parents should not know there was one possible place in Jerusalem for him. Clarke renders them my Father's concerns but reports the house translation as defended by Grotius and Pearce and read by the Syriac, the later Persic and the Armenian, a child being looked for in his father's house. Barnes mentions the same alternative but keeps the business. Ellicott keeps the literal sense, the things that are my Father's, holding its vague width to cover the house as well, and calls it a prophecy of the consciousness of direct Sonship which the later life manifests. Calvin takes the doctrine, that whatever we owe to men must yield to the first table of the law, so we obey kings and parents only in subjection to God.

That the parents understood not is the hardest admission in the chapter. Ellicott grants that sceptical criticism finds here a contradiction with the Annunciation, and answers that twelve years of ordinary childhood may have dulled the impressions and that the writer was conscious of no inconsistency; he sets the restraint of the record against the apocryphal gospels, where the child moulds sparrows of clay and claps them into flight and strikes a playmate dumb. The Greek Exposition finds three things in the subjection that follows, the love of God, honour to parents, and the preferring of God to parents. Ambrose calls that subjection a mark not of weakness but of filial duty, since he was obedient to a handmaid and to his pretended father. Cyril answers the Eunomian heretics, that it is not the Word but the Word made flesh which is said to increase, the perfect nature being not enlarged but by degrees manifested, since the law of nature does not brook higher faculties than a man's age permits; Theophylact says it more shortly, that the showing forth of his wisdom is his increase.
